newsitem.title: HONG KONG: BT Fund Mgrs sees dlr at 120 yen in 6-12 months.
newsitem.headline: BT Fund Mgrs sees dlr at 120 yen in 6-12 months.

text.p: The U.S. dollar could rise to 120 yen in the next six to 12 months as the U.S. economy grows strongly and Japan suffers from structural inefficiences, Dirk Morris, currency manager at BT Fund Managers, said on Monday.
"The U.S. dollar will continue to strengthen against major currencies both on valuation and interest rate differential grounds," Morris told reporters in Hong Kong.

"The recent stronger-than-expected growth in the U.S. could lead to higher interest rates, while Europe and Japan are still struggling to sustain normal growth rates, applying pressure for lower interest rates," he said.
Morris expects the dollar to top 115 yen over the next couple of months and rise to 120 yen in the next six to 12 months. The dollar was at 110.50 yen on Monday.

Morris sees the U.S. Federal Reserve raising the federal funds rate 25 basis points to 5.50 percent at its September 24 policy making meeting and he predicts another 25 to 50 basis point tightening after U.S. presidental elections in November.
"Over the next year I see short rates at about six percent versus about five percent now," he said.
The dollar will rise to 1.55 marks within three months and will push past 160 marks in 12 months, Morris predicted, though much would depend on the outlook for European monetary union.
The dollar is trading around 1.51 marks now.

As other countries pressure Japan to open its economy, some sectors are facing stiff import competition because of their inability to compete effectively. That will continue to pressure the yen, said Morris.
Like Japan, other Asian countries also have structural problems that will pressure their currencies versus the dollar.
"For example, the recent high levels of capital spending in Korea and Thailand require continued export growth to pay increasing debt burdens," Morris said.

"As export growth in these countries has slowed this year, current account imbalances have become unsustainable, leading to currency depreciations and the tightening of domestic policies to curtail imports," he said.

The high level of intra-Asian trade makes the risks of a more widespread economic slowdown in the region even greater, as policies to reduce imports in some Asian countries hurt exports of neighboring countries, Morris added.
Morris said Korea would find it difficult to compete if the yen falls to 120 per dollar as he envisions. In such a case, the won could drop to 900 per dollar, he said.
The won currently is trading at about 829 to the dollar.
Other Asian currencies are unlikely to make much headway against the dollar, and Morris predicts that most will soften against the U.S. unit, albeit modestly.
"Asian currencies will have a difficult time appreciating much against the dollar, but they will be going up against the yen," he noted.
For Indonesia's rupiah, politics are the biggest issue. "But politics aside, I think the rupiah will depreciate slightly but will stay toward the top end of its new band," said Morris.

Asked about the Hong Kong dollar's vulnerablity to speculation ahead of the handover of sovereignty to China in mid 1997, Morris said "international investors will be very, very cautious ahead of next year."
He said the market's thin liquidity and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's huge reserves to back up the currency should discourage attacks on the Hong Kong dollar.
BT Fund Managers represents Bankers Trust's international fund management activities in Asia.
